title: Which one is banana man? Evaluating vision–language models in multi-turn pragmatic interpretation
one_sentence: VLMs can exploit externally supplied, game-specific Tangram conventions but often fail to accumulate useful context or recover from their own errors under limited feedback, separating convention retrieval from construction and repair.
problem: Can vision-language models pragmatically interpret conventionalized descriptions across multiple turns, and how do context amount, order, relevance, and feedback quality affect that ability relative to humans?
method: Using ten 2–6-player, six-round Tangram games and naïve human matcher data, the study evaluates five open-weight VLMs across eight context conditions and three feedback regimes. New human samples cover backward and random order; model analyses compare interactive limited feedback, human-yoked limited feedback, and full feedback, with bootstrap intervals and additional frontier-model checks.
findings: Models improved substantially when correct, relevant prior mappings were supplied and could approach human or near-ceiling performance under human-yoked or full feedback.
With their own guesses plus only correct/incorrect feedback, models improved little and performed at or below chance after a prior mistake, while naïve humans corrected roughly half of prior errors.

Context from the same game and prior instances of the same tangram mattered most; other-game or target-ablated context produced much lower performance, supporting retrieval of convention-specific mappings more than general task learning.
Images helped most early or when contextual mappings were sparse; later performance was often similar without images, and trial-level model-human correspondence remained weak.
real_contribution: Provides a causal decomposition of convention retrieval, context relevance, feedback use, and error recovery for VLM pragmatic interpretation, filling a distinct role from dyad-generation and pseudo-dyad studies.
biggest_weakness: Models act as naïve interpreters of archived human games rather than reciprocal partners; interactive feedback supplies correctness without the correct answer, and many analyses aggregate heterogeneous models and items.
claim_boundary: Shows that tested VLMs can retrieve externally available mappings yet struggle to bootstrap and repair them in this constrained overhearer task; it does not establish that all models cannot form conventions or that retrieval alone is grounding.
why_researcher_should_care: It is the clearest current precedent for the AMSC distinction between having a convention in context and causally building, revising, and repairing one through interaction.
